title: Integral polynomial orbit coefficients for a lowest-weight SL2 vector
statement:
Let $B$ be a commutative ring, $q\geq0$ an integer, and $V=\bigoplus_{i=0}^q V_i$ a finite free $B$-module with specified finite free summands [def-weil-pbc-free-module, def-weil-pbc-direct-sum-modules]. Let $\rho$ be a representation of $\operatorname{SL}_{2,B}$ on $V$: for every commutative $B$-algebra $C$ it gives a group homomorphism $\rho_C:\{g\in\operatorname{Mat}_2(C):\det g=1\}\to\operatorname{Aut}_C(C\otimes_B V)$, natural in $C$, whose matrix entries are regular functions in $B[a,b,c,d]/(ad-bc-1)$. Tensor products have the meaning of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Put $x_+(z)=I_2+zE_{12}$, $x_-(z)=I_2+zE_{21}$, $h(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$, and $w=x_+(1)x_-(-1)x_+(1)$, where $I_2$ is the identity matrix and $E_{ij}$ has its only nonzero entry $1$ at position $(i,j)$. Assume $\rho_C(h(t))$ acts on $C\otimes_B V_i$ as multiplication by $t^{2i-q}$ for every $C$ and every unit $t\in C$. Let $v\in V_0$ be fixed by every $\rho_C(x_-(z))$ after scalar extension.

There are unique vectors $v_i\in V_i$, with $v_0=v$, such that $\rho_{B[z]}(x_+(z))v=\sum_{i=0}^q z^i v_i$. For all $C$, all $z\in C$ and $0\leq i\leq q$, they satisfy
$$\rho_C(x_+(z))v_i=\sum_{j=0}^{q-i}\binom{i+j}{j}z^jv_{i+j},\qquad
\rho_C(x_-(z))v_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom{q-i+j}{j}z^jv_{i-j},\qquad
\rho_C(w)v_i=(-1)^i v_{q-i}.$$
Here vectors on the right are mapped to $C\otimes_B V$. In particular the coefficient of $z$ in $\rho(x_+(z))v_i$ is $(i+1)v_{i+1}$ when $i<q$. The identities commute with arbitrary and successive base changes. No nonzero, spanning or primitivity condition is imposed on the $v_i$, and no factorial is inverted.

source.place: Propositions 22.14 and 22.15, printed pp.466--467, motivate polynomial orbit coefficients and Weyl reversal. The arbitrary-ring binomial identities are an agent generalization proved by coefficient comparison in the SL2 Gauss identity, not a quotation of these field statements.

proof.text: Choose the union of bases of the specified summands as a basis of $V$. Substitute $a=d=1$, $b=T$, $c=0$ in the regular matrix entries of $\rho$. Applied to $v$, this gives a finite polynomial $P(T)=\sum_{n\geq0}T^n a_n$ with $a_n\in V$. Here and below $V[T]$ means finite formal sums with coefficients in $V$; the basis identifies it with $B[T]\otimes_B V$, so coefficients are unique. Naturality gives $\rho_C(x_+(z))(1\otimes v)=\sum_n z^n(1\otimes a_n)$ for every $B$-algebra $C$ and $z\in C$. Evaluation at $T=0$ gives $a_0=v$.

source.place: Printed p.466, paragraph preceding Proposition 22.14: polynomial expansion; arbitrary-ring version by substitution in the given matrix entries.

proof.text:
Write $a_n=\sum_{i=0}^q a_{n,i}$ in the given direct sum. Over $B[T,U,U^{-1}]$, the matrix identity $h(U)x_+(T)=x_+(U^2T)h(U)$ and the weight of $v$ give
$$\sum_{n,i}T^nU^{2i-q}a_{n,i}=\sum_{n,i}T^nU^{2n-q}a_{n,i}.$$
Compare the $i$-th component and then Laurent coefficients. If $i\ne n$, the coefficient of $T^nU^{2i-q}$ says $a_{n,i}=0$. Laurent coefficients are independent over any $B$: multiplying a finite Laurent sum by a large power of $U$ gives an ordinary polynomial with the same coefficients. Thus $a_n\in V_n$ for $n\leq q$ and $a_n=0$ for $n>q$. Set $v_i=a_i$.

source.place: Printed p.466, Proposition 22.14, conjugation and weight comparison, performed at a universal unit instead of points of a field.

proof.text: Any list in the assertion must give the polynomial $P(T)$ after taking $C=B[T]$ and $z=T$; equality of formal coefficients makes that list equal to $(v_i)_{i=0}^q$. The expansion from the preceding steps therefore proves existence and uniqueness, with $v_0=v$.

source.place: Printed p.466, Proposition 22.14, constant term and uniqueness in the universal-polynomial formulation.

proof.text:
Over $B[S,T]$, the identity $x_+(S)x_+(T)=x_+(S+T)$ gives
$$\sum_{i=0}^q T^i\rho(x_+(S))v_i=\sum_{k=0}^q(S+T)^k v_k.$$
Apply the cited binomial expansion in the commutative ring $B[S,T]$. The coefficient of $T^i$ on the right is $\sum_{k=i}^q\binom{k}{i}S^{k-i}v_k$. Put $k=i+j$; the integer equality $\binom{i+j}{i}=\binom{i+j}{j}$ follows by interchanging the two factorials in its defining formula. This is the asserted upper-root formula over $B[S]$.

source.place: Agent supplement to Proposition 22.14: upper-root addition and polynomial coefficient comparison.

proof.text:
Put $A=B[S,T]$ and $u=1+ST$. In $A[u^{-1}]$, direct multiplication gives
$$x_-(S)x_+(T)=x_+(T/u)h(u^{-1})x_-(S/u).$$
Indeed the first two factors on the right have rows $(u^{-1},T)$ and $(0,u)$, so the complete product has rows $(1,T)$ and $(S,u)$, as does the left side. The rightmost factor fixes $v$ by hypothesis, and $h(u^{-1})v=u^qv$. Hence in this algebra the representation identity becomes
$$\sum_{i=0}^qT^i\rho(x_-(S))v_i=\sum_{k=0}^q T^k u^{q-k}v_k.$$
All exponents $q-k$ are nonnegative; both displayed sides are vector polynomials already over $A$.

source.place: Agent SL2 Gauss matrix calculation supplementing Proposition 22.14; all fixed-vector and torus hypotheses applied over the displayed B-algebra.

proof.text: The map $V[S,T]\longrightarrow A[u^{-1}]\otimes_B V$ is injective. To see this explicitly, multiplication by $u$ on any vector polynomial $F=\sum_{r\geq0}T^r f_r(S)$ is injective: the equation $uF=0$ gives $f_0=0$ and $f_r+Sf_{r-1}=0$ for $r\geq1$, so induction gives every $f_r=0$. Every power of $u$ is consequently injective. In a basis of $V$, vanishing after localization means each of its finitely many polynomial coordinates is killed by a power of $u$ (the equality criterion for fractions); a common power kills $F$, whence $F=0$. Thus the identity of the preceding step holds in $V[S,T]$. This argument assumes no domain or reducedness property of $B$.

source.place: Agent elementary denominator check for the preceding Gauss identity: coefficient recursion for multiplication by 1+ST.

proof.text:
Expand $(1+ST)^{q-k}$ using the cited binomial formula. The coefficient of $T^i$ in $T^k(1+ST)^{q-k}$ is zero for $k>i$, and is $\binom{q-k}{i-k}S^{i-k}$ for $k\leq i$. Comparing $T^i$ coefficients in the identity now proved over $A$ yields
$$\rho(x_-(S))v_i=\sum_{k=0}^i\binom{q-k}{i-k}S^{i-k}v_k.$$
Writing $j=i-k$ gives exactly $\sum_{j=0}^i\binom{q-i+j}{j}S^jv_{i-j}$, the lower-root formula. No coefficient or factorial was cancelled.

source.place: Agent supplement to Proposition 22.14: lower-root Gauss identity, binomial expansion and coefficient comparison.

proof.text:
The definition of $w$ gives the matrix with rows $(0,1)$ and $(-1,0)$. Over $B[T,T^{-1}]$ one has
$$w x_+(T)=x_+(-T^{-1})h(-T^{-1})x_-(T^{-1}).$$
Indeed the product on the right has rows $(0,1)$ and $(-1,-T)$, equal to those of the left side. Apply the representation to $v$: the last factor fixes $v$, and the middle factor acts on $v$ by $(-T^{-1})^{-q}=(-T)^q$. Consequently
$$\sum_{i=0}^qT^i\rho(w)v_i=(-T)^qP(-T^{-1})=\sum_{k=0}^q(-1)^{q+k}T^{q-k}v_k.$$
Comparing Laurent coefficients at $T^i$ gives $\rho(w)v_i=(-1)^{2q-i}v_{q-i}=(-1)^iv_{q-i}$, since the two sign exponents differ by $2(q-i)$.

source.place: Printed pp.466–467, Lemma 22.15 motivates reversal; agent explicit Weyl factorization fixes the sign over arbitrary rings.

proof.text: Evaluate the polynomial upper- and lower-root identities at $S=z$ under the $B$-algebra homomorphism $B[S]\to C$ for any $C$ and $z\in C$. Naturality of $\rho$ identifies their left sides with the requested actions over $C$ and their coefficients with $1\otimes v_i$. The same naturality applies to the constant matrix $w$. In the upper-root formula, the coefficient of $S$ when $i<q$ is $\binom{i+1}{1}v_{i+1}=(i+1)v_{i+1}$, since $\binom{i+1}{1}=i+1$.

source.place: Agent specialization of the universal identities; Proposition 22.14 polynomial-orbit interpretation.

proof.text: For $B\to D$, apply the map $b\mapsto b\cdot1_D$ to every polynomial coordinate constructed above. The orbit becomes $\sum_i T^i(1\otimes v_i)$; uniqueness of its coefficients shows that these are precisely the vectors constructed for the scalar-extended representation and the specified summands $D\otimes_B V_i$. For $B\to D\to E$, the tensor comparison sends $e\otimes(d\otimes v_i)$ to $ed\otimes v_i$, as follows from the bilinear universal property. Thus one-step and successive base changes give the same coefficients, and each displayed identity maps to the corresponding identity over the new base. This uses no injectivity or flatness of $B\to D$. Zero vectors and vanishing binomial coefficients cause no change to any coefficient comparison.

source.place: Agent arbitrary and successive base-change check, using only coordinate substitution and the tensor universal property.
